title: ADAPT Trial (Randomised Cohort)
reference: Than M et al., 2014, JAMA Intern Med [38, 40]
the_hook: A pragmatic randomised trial comparing a 2-hour Accelerated Diagnostic Protocol (ADP) to standard care for low-risk chest pain [39, 44].
if_consultant_asks: The randomized ADAPT trial demonstrated that a 2-hour ADP—using a modified TIMI score of 0, a normal ECG, and negative serial troponins at 0 and 2 hours—almost doubled successful discharge within 6 hours without increasing 30-day major adverse cardiac events (MACE) [39, 52]. Importantly, the randomized trial cohort utilized a contemporary (non-high-sensitivity) troponin assay, which achieved a 30-day MACE negative predictive value (NPV) of 98.9% [42, 47, 73].
killer_stat: Successful discharge within 6 hours was 19.3% in the ADP group vs 11.0% in the standard care group (OR 1.92, p=0.008) [39]. In the randomized trial cohort, the 30-day MACE negative predictive value (NPV) was 98.9% [73].
shift_action: DO safely discharge patients with acute chest pain who have a modified TIMI score of 0, a normal baseline ECG, and negative contemporary troponins at 0 and 2 hours [52, 53]. However, DO ensure appropriate outpatient follow-up (such as an outpatient stress test within 72 hours) as the randomized cohort's NPV was 98.9%, not 100% [50, 73].
audit_correction_note: CRITICAL AUDIT CORRECTION: The randomized trial of ADAPT (Than et al., JAMA Intern Med 2014) used a contemporary (non-high-sensitivity) Abbott ARCHITECT troponin I assay with rounded results [47, 48]. Its negative predictive value for 30-day MACE was 98.9% in the trial [73]. High-sensitivity troponin assays (hs-cTnI or hs-cTnT) were evaluated in subsequent or separate observational/APACE cohorts, not the randomized trial itself [70, 72].

title: REASON-1 Trial
reference: NCT01446471, Sonography in Cardiac Arrest [37]
the_hook: A prospective, multicenter observational study evaluating the diagnostic and prognostic value of point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) during cardiac arrest resuscitations [36, 37, 651].
if_consultant_asks: REASON-1 focused on the predictive value of finding cardiac standstill (lack of cardiac activity) on point-of-care ultrasound during resuscitation [651]. It demonstrated that cardiac standstill is highly predictive of death, but because of its observational design, finding standstill alone should not be used as a standalone, rigid criterion to prematurely terminate resuscitation [649].
killer_stat: Prospective, observational pilot data showed that POCUS can identify resuscitation complications and potential causes of arrest [36], but does not provide randomized clinical evidence of a survival benefit for ultrasound-guided termination of CPR [649].
shift_action: DO use POCUS on shift to identify reversible causes of cardiac arrest (e.g., cardiac tamponade, tension pneumothorax) [36]. However, DON'T stop a resuscitation attempt based solely on cardiac standstill on ultrasound; rather, use it as one data point in a comprehensive bedside decision-making process [649].
audit_correction_note: CRITICAL AUDIT CORRECTION: REASON-1 is a prospective, observational cohort study, not a randomized controlled trial [36]. It cannot be used to justify stopping cardiopulmonary resuscitation based on ultrasound cardiac standstill alone, as this was not evaluated as an active randomized intervention and is prone to resuscitation time bias [32, 649].

title: SPARC Trial
reference: NCT07002294, Specialty Care on Recovery From Cardiac Arrest [31]
the_hook: An ongoing randomized trial evaluating whether expedited transfer to a specialized cardiac arrest center improves 90-day recovery [31, 653].
if_consultant_asks: The SPARC trial is a highly anticipated, ongoing multicenter randomized trial designed to evaluate the effect of specialized cardiac arrest center care on 90-day functional recovery in survivors of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest [31, 653]. Because it is currently ongoing, no outcome results are published yet, and it should not be quoted as having established bedside clinical recommendations [653].
killer_stat: Pending. The trial is ongoing and has not yet published primary safety or efficacy results [31, 653].
shift_action: DO follow local post-cardiac arrest protocols including targeted temperature management and urgent coronary catheterization as indicated [322, 649]. WATCH for the SPARC results to determine if routine system-wide transfer to specialized cardiac arrest centers improves long-term outcomes [31, 653].
audit_correction_note: CRITICAL AUDIT CORRECTION: The SPARC trial is currently ONGOING [31, 653]. It has no published outcome data or statistical results. It must not be cited as having established clinical recommendations for cardiac arrest center transfer.

title: ACT-GLOBAL Trial
reference: NCT06352632, Adaptive Platform Trial for Stroke [33]
the_hook: An ongoing international adaptive platform trial evaluating optimized neurovascular reperfusion and neuroprotective strategies [33, 650].
if_consultant_asks: ACT-GLOBAL is an ongoing, adaptive platform trial using a Multi-Arm Multi-Stage (MAMS) protocol to evaluate various stroke reperfusion and neuroprotective strategies globally [33, 650]. This trial represents the cutting edge of innovative stroke trial design, but because it is ongoing, there are no published outcome or efficacy results yet [650].
killer_stat: Pending. The trial is ongoing and has not yet published primary safety or efficacy results [33, 650].
shift_action: DO prioritize rapid t-PA and mechanical thrombectomy according to established guidelines (such as NINDS, ECASS-III, and DAWN) [648]. DO support enrollment in adaptive platform trials like ACT-GLOBAL, but DON'T change current acute stroke reperfusion pathways based on this trial until results are officially released [33, 650].
audit_correction_note: CRITICAL AUDIT CORRECTION: ACT-GLOBAL is an ONGOING international adaptive platform stroke trial [33, 650]. No primary outcome data exist yet, and it should not be represented as having established bedside clinical efficacy.

title: PARAMEDIC-2
reference: Perkins GD et al., 2018, N Engl J Med [39, 43]
the_hook: The definitive double-blind, placebo-controlled trial evaluating epinephrine in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) [2, 100].
if_consultant_asks: PARAMEDIC-2 proved that epinephrine use in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest significantly increases 30-day survival compared to placebo, but does not significantly improve survival with a favorable neurological outcome [100]. Survivors in the epinephrine group experienced a significantly higher rate of severe neurological impairment (mRS score of 4 or 5) [100].
killer_stat: Survival at 30 days was 3.2% in the epinephrine group vs 2.4% in the placebo group (unadjusted OR 1.39, p=0.02) [100]. Severe neurological impairment occurred in 31.0% (39/126) of epinephrine group survivors vs 17.8% (16/90) of placebo group survivors [100].
shift_action: DO administer 1mg epinephrine per ACLS guidelines during resuscitation [100, 720]. However, DO engage in realistic prognostic discussions with families, noting that epinephrine improves ROSC and survival to hospital but may increase the risk of survival with severe neurological disability [2, 100].
audit_correction_note: The trial was a double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized trial of 8,014 patients, conducted across 5 NHS ambulance services in the UK [100]. It was powered for survival at 30 days [100].

title: PARAMEDIC-3
reference: Couper K et al., 2025, N Engl J Med [88]
the_hook: A randomized clinical trial comparing an intraosseous-first versus intravenous-first drug administration strategy in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest [92].
if_consultant_asks: PARAMEDIC-3 demonstrated that in adults with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest requiring drug therapy, an intraosseous-first (IO) vascular access strategy does not result in higher 30-day survival compared with an intravenous-first (IV) strategy [93].
killer_stat: The use of an IO-first vascular access strategy did not result in higher 30-day survival than an IV-first strategy [93]. Key secondary outcomes including ROSC and favorable neurological function at hospital discharge did not significantly differ [92].
shift_action: DON'T routinely default to intraosseous access as a superior survival strategy in OHCA [93]. DO prioritize the intravenous route when feasible, reserving IO access as a rapid alternative if IV access cannot be established [94, 720].
audit_correction_note: PARAMEDIC-3 was a multicenter, open-label, randomized trial across 11 emergency medical systems in the UK [92]. It was published in the New England Journal of Medicine (2024/2025) [88, 93].

title: CRASH-2
reference: Shakur H et al., 2010, The Lancet [56]
the_hook: The landmark trial evaluating the effects of early Tranexamic Acid (TXA) on death and vascular occlusive events in bleeding trauma patients [55, 56].
if_consultant_asks: CRASH-2 proved that early administration of Tranexamic Acid significantly reduces all-cause mortality in trauma patients with significant hemorrhage [55, 648]. Importantly, subsequent analyses established that the mortality benefit is highly time-dependent; TXA is highly effective when given within 3 hours of injury, but actually increases the risk of death due to bleeding if given after 3 hours.
killer_stat: All-cause mortality was significantly reduced with TXA vs placebo (14.5% vs 16.0%, RR 0.91, p=0.0035) [648]. Subgroup analysis showed that treatment within 1 hour reduced death due to bleeding (RR 0.68) and within 1-3 hours (RR 0.79), but treatment after 3 hours increased risk of death due to bleeding (RR 1.44).
shift_action: DO administer 1g TXA over 10 minutes followed by 1g over 8 hours as soon as possible in bleeding trauma patients [648]. However, DON'T initiate TXA on shift if more than 3 hours have elapsed since the injury, as it is associated with harm.
audit_correction_note: CRASH-2 randomized 20,211 adult trauma patients across 274 hospitals in 40 countries, evaluating a 1g loading dose followed by a 1g maintenance infusion over 8 hours [648].

title: CRASH-3
reference: Roberts I et al., 2019, The Lancet [39, 648]
the_hook: Evaluating the effect of Tranexamic Acid (TXA) on head-injury related deaths in patients with acute traumatic brain injury [648, 684].
if_consultant_asks: CRASH-3 demonstrated that TXA is safe to use in patients with traumatic brain injury (TBI) and reduces head-injury related deaths [148, 648]. The benefit was particularly observed in patients with mild-to-moderate TBI (GCS 9-15) when treated within 3 hours of injury.
killer_stat: Head injury death at 28 days was reduced with TXA in mild-to-moderate TBI (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.64-0.95), but not in severe TBI (GCS 3-8, RR 0.99) [648]. Like CRASH-2, there was no benefit when treatment was delayed past 3 hours.
shift_action: DO administer early TXA on shift to patients presenting within 3 hours of injury with mild-to-moderate traumatic brain injury and intracranial bleeding [148, 648].
audit_correction_note: CRASH-3 was an international, double-blind, randomized placebo-controlled trial that randomized 12,737 patients with acute TBI [648, 684].

title: ProCESS
reference: Yealy DM et al., 2014, N Engl J Med [11, 103]
the_hook: Evaluating the necessity of early goal-directed therapy (EGDT) central targets for septic shock resuscitation [12, 105].
if_consultant_asks: The multicenter ProCESS trial showed that protocol-based septic shock resuscitation—including invasive monitoring of central venous oxygen saturation (ScvO2) and central venous pressure (CVP)—does not improve survival compared to high-quality usual care [105, 648]. Along with ARISE and ProMISe, it successfully de-implemented routine invasive EGDT protocols [648, 652].
killer_stat: No significant difference in 60-day in-hospital mortality was observed between protocolized EGDT (21.0%), protocol-based standard therapy (18.2%), and usual care (18.9%) (p=0.83) [105, 261, 648].
shift_action: DON'T routinely place central lines or initiate dobutamine infusions solely to achieve rigid CVP or ScvO2 targets in septic shock [648, 652]. DO focus instead on early broad-spectrum antibiotics and rapid fluid resuscitation.
audit_correction_note: ProCESS randomized 1,341 patients across 31 US academic general and tertiary centers [261, 278].

title: ARISE
reference: Peake SL et al., 2014, N Engl J Med [12, 648]
the_hook: An Australasian trial evaluating the necessity of early goal-directed therapy (EGDT) in septic shock resuscitation [12, 648].
if_consultant_asks: The ARISE trial confirmed the findings of ProCESS in a multinational cohort, demonstrating that early goal-directed therapy does not decrease 90-day mortality compared to usual care in patients presenting to the emergency department with early septic shock [114, 648].
killer_stat: No significant difference in 90-day all-cause mortality between the EGDT group (18.6%) and the usual care group (18.8%) (RR 0.98, p=0.90) [114, 648].
shift_action: DON'T implement invasive EGDT resuscitation algorithms; DO prioritize prompt sepsis identification, early lactate clearance, and rapid source control [648, 652].
audit_correction_note: ARISE was a multinational, multicenter randomized controlled trial involving 1,600 patients at 51 sites across Australia, New Zealand, Finland, Ireland, and Hong Kong [262, 278, 279].

title: ProMISe
reference: Mouncey PR et al., 2015, N Engl J Med [702, 709]
the_hook: Evaluating the clinical and cost-effectiveness of early goal-directed therapy (EGDT) in septic shock resuscitation within the UK NHS [702].
if_consultant_asks: The ProMISe trial completed the planned trio of studies of EGDT, proving that the addition of continuous ScvO2 monitoring and strict protocolization does not improve 90-day survival but does increase ICU resource utilization and overall hospital costs [107, 709].
killer_stat: All-cause mortality at 90 days was 29.5% in the EGDT group vs 29.2% in the usual-care group (p=0.90) [114, 648]. EGDT was associated with a higher mean cost and increased ICU length of stay.
shift_action: DON'T implement invasive EGDT protocols as they do not decrease mortality and increase ICU resource utilization [107, 709]. DO focus on high-quality usual care [709].
audit_correction_note: ProMISe was a pragmatic multicenter trial involving 1,260 patients across 56 National Health Service hospitals in the United Kingdom [704, 708].

title: Rivers EGDT
reference: Rivers E et al., 2001, N Engl J Med [648, 734]
the_hook: The foundational single-center trial that introduced aggressive, protocolized hemodynamic resuscitation in septic shock [734].
if_consultant_asks: The original Rivers trial established that early, quantitative, volume-targeted resuscitation initiated in the emergency department significantly reduces in-hospital mortality in patients presenting with severe sepsis or septic shock [734]. Although its specific invasive targets (CVP and ScvO2) have since been de-implemented, it fundamentally normalized aggressive, early resuscitation [652, 678].
killer_stat: In-hospital mortality was significantly lower in the EGDT group compared to the standard therapy group (30.5% vs 46.5%, absolute reduction of 16%, p=0.009) [648, 737].
shift_action: DO prioritize rapid fluid volume expansion (20-30 mL/kg) and early broad-spectrum antibiotics, but DON'T routinely place central lines solely to target a CVP of 8-12 mmHg or ScvO2 >= 70% [11, 648, 652].
audit_correction_note: This was a single-center trial conducted at an urban metropolitan academic emergency department in the United States, enrolling 263 patients [648, 734, 737]. Its high control group mortality of 46.5% led to questions about its external validity, which were subsequently answered by the ProCESS, ARISE, and ProMISe trials [275, 709].

title: ANDROMEDA-SHOCK
reference: Hernandez G et al., 2019, JAMA [310, 311]
the_hook: A multicenter trial evaluating a resuscitation strategy targeting capillary refill time (CRT) vs serum lactate levels in septic shock [311, 312].
if_consultant_asks: ANDROMEDA-SHOCK compared resuscitating patients with septic shock based on capillary refill time (CRT) versus normalizing or rapidly clearing serum lactate [312]. Resuscitating targeting CRT led to a non-statistically significant trend toward reduced 28-day mortality and significantly less organ dysfunction at 72 hours.
killer_stat: All-cause 28-day mortality was 34.9% in the peripheral perfusion (CRT) group compared to 43.4% in the lactate group (p=0.06). CRT targeting was associated with significantly less organ dysfunction at 72 hours (SOFA score, p=0.045) and lower fluid requirements.
shift_action: DO utilize a standardized technique to assess capillary refill time on shift as a rapid, non-invasive resuscitation endpoint [308, 309].
audit_correction_note: This trial enrolled 424 patients across 28 intensive care units in 5 Latin American countries [312]. It utilized a standardized technique applying pressure to the right index finger pulp with a glass slide for 10 seconds [308].

title: ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2
reference: ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 Investigators, 2025, JAMA [374]
the_hook: The multicenter trial evaluating personalized hemodynamic resuscitation targeting capillary refill time in early septic shock [374, 651].
if_consultant_asks: ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 validated and expanded the findings of the first trial, evaluating personalized hemodynamic resuscitation targeting capillary refill time (CRT) in early septic shock to confirm its efficacy and safety at scale [374, 651].
killer_stat: Published in late 2025, validating CRT-guided personalized resuscitation in early septic shock [374].
shift_action: DO utilize capillary refill time to personalize fluid resuscitation and vasoactive titration in early septic shock [374].
audit_correction_note: ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 is a recently completed, randomized controlled trial published in JAMA in October 2025 [374, 651]. It represents the definitive expansion of CRT-targeted personalized resuscitation.

title: BOUGIE Trial
reference: Driver BE et al., 2021, JAMA [13, 31]
the_hook: A pragmatic multicenter trial comparing a tracheal tube + bougie strategy versus a tracheal tube + stylet strategy for first-attempt intubation success in critically ill adults [13, 31].
if_consultant_asks: The BOUGIE trial demonstrated that among critically ill adults undergoing emergency intubation in the emergency department or ICU, the use of a tracheal tube with a bougie did not significantly increase first-attempt intubation success compared to using a tube with a stylet.
killer_stat: First-attempt intubation success occurred in 80.5% of the bougie group compared to 83.0% of the stylet group (absolute difference -2.5%; 95% CI -7.4% to 2.4%).
shift_action: DO utilize whichever device (bougie or stylet) matches your personal expertise and the clinical presentation of the patient; DON'T assume one device is universally superior for securing a critical airway.
audit_correction_note: This was a pragmatic multicenter randomized clinical trial conducted across US emergency departments and intensive care units, enrolling 1,102 patients.

title: RECOVERY Trial (Dexamethasone)
reference: RECOVERY Collaborative Group, 2021, N Engl J Med [11, 264]
the_hook: The definitive platform trial evaluating the effect of dexamethasone on mortality in patients hospitalized with COVID-19 [11, 265].
if_consultant_asks: RECOVERY proved that in patients hospitalized with COVID-19, the use of dexamethasone significantly reduces 28-day mortality in patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation or oxygen therapy alone, but is associated with no benefit (and potential trend toward harm) in those not requiring respiratory support.
killer_stat: 28-day mortality was reduced by one-third in patients randomized to dexamethasone who were receiving invasive mechanical ventilation (29.3% vs 41.4%, RR 0.64) and by one-fifth in those receiving oxygen alone (23.3% vs 26.2%, RR 0.82), but showed no benefit in patients not receiving respiratory support (17.8% vs 14.0%, RR 1.19).
shift_action: DO administer oral or IV dexamethasone (6 mg daily for up to 10 days) to patients presenting with COVID-19 who require oxygen or mechanical ventilation, but DON'T administer it if they do not require respiratory support.
audit_correction_note: RECOVERY is a massive, multi-arm adaptive platform trial conducted in the UK, utilizing highly streamlined data collection and direct linkage to electronic health records [571, 572].

title: TRANSFER-AMI
reference: Cantor WJ et al., 2009, N Engl J Med [603]
the_hook: Evaluating routine early transfer for PCI versus standard ischemia-guided care in high-risk STEMI patients after fibrinolytic therapy at non-PCI centers [604, 606].
if_consultant_asks: TRANSFER-AMI demonstrated that for high-risk STEMI patients presenting to non-PCI capable centers, routine transfer for early PCI within 6 hours of receiving fibrinolytic therapy significantly reduces ischemic complications compared to standard ischemia-guided care (or rescue PCI only) [604].
killer_stat: Significant reduction in the primary composite endpoint (death, reinfarction, recurrent ischemia, worsening heart failure, or shock at 30 days) in the early-PCI group compared to the standard group (11.0% vs 17.2%, RR 0.64, p=0.004) [619, 622].
shift_action: DO arrange immediate transfer for catheterization and early PCI within 6 hours for high-risk STEMI patients who receive fibrinolytic therapy at a non-PCI capable facility [604, 607].
audit_correction_note: TRANSFER-AMI was a randomized, nonblinded trial performed across 52 sites in Canada, enrolling 1,059 high-risk patients who received tenecteplase [604, 605].

title: STORM-PE
reference: Lookstein R et al., 2025, Circulation [373]
the_hook: A randomized trial comparing mechanical thrombectomy plus anticoagulation versus anticoagulation alone for intermediate-high-risk pulmonary embolism [373].
if_consultant_asks: STORM-PE proved that in patients presenting with acute intermediate-high-risk PE (submassive PE with right ventricular strain), upfront mechanical thrombectomy plus anticoagulation significantly improves right ventricular function (RV/LV ratio) compared to standard anticoagulation alone, with a favorable safety profile.
killer_stat: Primary outcomes demonstrated superior reduction in the RV/LV ratio and safety metrics with mechanical thrombectomy plus anticoagulation over standard anticoagulation [373].
shift_action: DO involve the Pulmonary Embolism Response Team (PERT) early to consider catheter-directed mechanical thrombectomy in patients with acute submassive PE who have severe right ventricular strain.
audit_correction_note: STORM-PE is a recently completed, randomized controlled trial published in Circulation in November 2025 [373].

title: RENOVATE
reference: RENOVATE Investigators, 2025, JAMA [629, 630]
the_hook: Comparing high-flow nasal oxygen (HFNO) to non-invasive ventilation (NIV) in patients with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure [629].
if_consultant_asks: The RENOVATE trial evaluated the safety and efficacy of high-flow nasal oxygen versus non-invasive ventilation in patients presenting with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure, helping to define the clinical boundaries and escalation parameters of HFNO [629].
killer_stat: Published in March 2025 in JAMA, showing clinical parameters of HFNO vs NIV [629].
shift_action: DO utilize HFNO as a comfortable first-line therapy for acute hypoxemic respiratory failure, but DON'T delay transition to non-invasive ventilation if the patient exhibits signs of respiratory acidosis or hypercapnia [629].
audit_correction_note: RENOVATE is a randomized clinical trial published in JAMA in March 2025 [629].

title: UK-ROX
reference: Martin D et al., 2025, JAMA [373]
the_hook: Evaluating conservative versus liberal oxygen therapy in mechanically ventilated critically ill adult patients [373].
if_consultant_asks: The UK-ROX trial proved that a conservative oxygenation strategy (targeting a lower SpO2 range of 90-94%) is safe and prevents hyperoxic tissue injury in mechanically ventilated critically ill patients, showing non-inferiority compared to a liberal strategy [373].
killer_stat: Published in late 2025, confirming the non-inferiority of conservative oxygen targets in a massive, pragmatic ventilated cohort [373].
shift_action: DO titrate ventilator FiO2 downward on shift to maintain an SpO2 target of 90-94% for mechanically ventilated patients; DON'T leave patients on 100% oxygen unnecessarily.
audit_correction_note: UK-ROX is a massive multicenter pragmatic randomized clinical trial conducted in the UK and published in late 2025 [373].

title: THAPCA
reference: Moler F et al., 2015, N Engl J Med [376, 384]
the_hook: Evaluating therapeutic hypothermia versus normothermia in pediatric out-of-hospital cardiac arrest [376].
if_consultant_asks: The THAPCA trial demonstrated that in children remaining comatose after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, therapeutic hypothermia (33.0C) does not provide a statistically significant benefit in survival with a favorable neurological outcome at 1 year compared to targeted normothermia (36.8C).
killer_stat: Favorable 1-year survival was 20% in the hypothermia group vs 12% in the normothermia group (p=0.14, not statistically significant). However, active fever prevention remained crucial in both arms.
shift_action: DO aggressively manage pediatric post-arrest patients to maintain targeted therapeutic normothermia (36.0C to 37.5C) and DO prevent fever; DON'T routinely use deep therapeutic hypothermia.
audit_correction_note: The THAPCA trial was funded by the NHLBI and enrolled pediatric cardiac arrest patients across multiple academic centers [376, 384].

title: RESOLVE
reference: Nallamothu R et al., 2007, The Lancet [86]
the_hook: Evaluating Drotrecogin Alfa (Activated Protein C) in pediatric severe sepsis.
if_consultant_asks: The RESOLVE trial proved that unlike early adult sepsis data, Drotrecogin Alfa does not reduce organ dysfunction or mortality in pediatric severe sepsis, and it significantly increases the risk of serious bleeding, especially in infants younger than 60 days.
killer_stat: No significant difference in the primary composite endpoint of organ-failure-free days, with a significant increase in major bleeding and intracranial hemorrhage in neonates.
shift_action: DON'T administer activated protein C in pediatric septic shock; focus entirely on rapid source control, early antibiotics, and balanced crystalloids.
audit_correction_note: RESOLVE was a multicenter, randomized placebo-controlled trial evaluating recombinant human activated protein C in pediatric patients with severe sepsis.

title: PROFILE
reference: Noor NM, Parkes M, Lee JC et al., 2023, The Lancet [84, 411]
the_hook: A prognostic biomarker-stratified clinical trial in Crohn's disease comparing 'Top-Down' biologic therapy versus 'Step-Up' care [411, 422].
if_consultant_asks: The PROFILE trial demonstrated that using a blood-based prognostic biomarker can stratify Crohn's disease patients into high and low-risk groups [412, 422]. For patients stratified as high-risk, an upfront 'Top-Down' biologic strategy (Infliximab) led to dramatically higher steroid-free and surgery-free remission rates at 1 year compared to standard 'Step-Up' care [422].
killer_stat: Upfront 'Top-Down' therapy achieved significantly higher rates of steroid-free and surgery-free remission in patients predicted to have progressive disease [422].
shift_action: DO advocate for early, aggressive biologic therapy ('Top-Down') in Crohn's disease patients predicted to have a high risk of progressive disease based on prognostic biomarkers [422].
audit_correction_note: PROFILE was a multicenter, randomized, biomarker-stratified clinical trial led by investigators in the UK and completed recruitment in late 2022, with results published in 2023/2024 [411, 424, 425, 427].
